Q: How to suppress "Restricted method called: java.lang.System::load" warning when using native-platform in Gradle on JDK 22+ A:

It looks like that warning is emitted by the Gradle launcher/client JVM, which reads its options from GRADLE_OPTS environment variable, so you should set it before executing of a gradle task:

export GRADLE_OPTS="--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED"

That works for Java 25 for sure, for 22 I did not test it, but it should be relevant as well.

Q: Defining local variable in Makefile target A:

Newer Make got a specialized function for creating local variables, $(let ):

zsh:
    $(let FILENAME,text.txt,\
        @echo "Copying $(FILENAME)...";\
        scp "$(FILENAME)" "user@host:/home/user/$(FILENAME)"\
    )

Note that multiline function invocations need trailing \ on every line except the last one. And since this is considered to be one line, all shell commands except the last one need trailing ;.

In older Make you can abuse foreach for this (with the exact same syntax, but replace let with foreach), but only if the variable value is a single word. Then there will only be one iteration, and foreach creates a magic local variable just like let does.

Alternatively, you can write to global variables from a recipe, choosing a sufficiently unique name to avoid conflicts. To do that, use this custom function:

override var = $(eval override $(subst #,$$(strip #),$(subst $,$$$$,$1)))
# Or a worse version for older Make, this doesn't handle # symbols:
#   override var = $(eval override $(subst $,$$$$,$1))

And then:

zsh:
    $(call var,__FILENAME := "text.txt")
    @echo "Copying $(__FILENAME)..."
    scp "$(__FILENAME)" "user@host:/home/user/$(__FILENAME)"

This is basically a wrapper for $(eval x = y) that handles $ and # in the value correctly.

You should prefix all the fake "local" variables with something (e.g. __ here) to avoid overwriting useful global variables. Overwriting old local variables from other recipes is not an issue, though.

Q: Send (mass) notification emails to users. What is the right way? A:

For sending: Resend, Postmark, Mailgun, SendGrid, Amazon SES.

They're similar in the part that matters — they own the sending IPs and their reputation, and they give you bounce and complaint webhooks instead of you parsing DSNs.

Resend is the least friction from Python, and its batch endpoint takes 100 messages per call, so the per-user loop you're worried about is 100 requests for a 10k announcement, not 10k.

Whichever you pick will hand you the SPF/DKIM/DMARC records to publish, and MXToolbox is the usual way to confirm they resolve.

Then check placement before the real send, because "delivered" in a provider dashboard only means the receiving server accepted the message: GlockApps and spamrate.is send to real Gmail/Outlook/Yahoo mailboxes and show whether it landed in the inbox, Promotions or spam.

Q: OpenSSH using private key on Windows ("Unprotected private key file" error) A:

Say you are logged in with an AzureAD administrator account and OpenSSH complains about your private key being unprotected:

    @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
    @         WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!          @
    @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@

Do the following in Powershell:

    $path = ".\path\to\privatekey.pem"
    $user = whoami
    
    icacls $path /setowner $user
    icacls $path /inheritance:r
    icacls $path /grant:r "${user}:(R)"
    icacls $path /remove:g "Everyone" "BUILTIN\Users" "BUILTIN\Administrators" "NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM"
    
    icacls $path

Q: Cybersecurity advice A:

Cybersecurity is such a broad field that trying to learn everything at once usually slows people down. A structured approach tends to work much better.

I'd suggest building your foundation first:

  • Strengthen your understanding of operating systems (especially Linux), networking, and basic programming (Python is a good choice).

  • Learn how common protocols such as HTTP, DNS, TCP/IP, and TLS work before diving into security tools.

  • Practice in legal lab environments such as virtual machines or intentionally vulnerable applications. Hands-on experience is far more valuable than only watching videos.

  • Study one area at a time (web security, network security, reverse engineering, cloud security, etc.) instead of jumping between topics.

Also, don't neglect defensive concepts. Understanding logging, monitoring, authentication, and secure system design will make you a stronger security professional than focusing only on offensive techniques
